Ten men. Healed in a single moment.
Only one came back.
And Jesus asked a question that still stings.
Where are the nine?
Luke, chapter seventeen.
Jesus is walking to Jerusalem, on the border of Samaria and Galilee.
At a village, ten lepers meet him.
But they stop far away. They have to.
The law told a leper to tear his clothes, cover his lip, and cry out: Unclean! Unclean!
And live alone, outside the camp.
So they shout across the distance. Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!
He does not touch them. He does not even say, be healed.
He says: Go, show yourselves to the priests.
So they go. Still covered in it.
And as they went, they were cleansed.
Nine of them keep walking. To the priest. To their families. To their old lives.
One turns back.
He praises God with a loud voice, and falls on his face at Jesus' feet.
And then Luke adds five words.
And he was a Samaritan.
The people the Jews had no dealings with.
Jesus asks: Were there not ten cleansed? But where are the nine?
None returned to give glory to God, except this stranger.
That word, stranger, in Greek, allo-gay-nays, appears nowhere else in the New Testament.
But in eighteen seventy one, it turned up carved in stone, in Jerusalem.
A warning from the Temple itself.
No foreigner may pass the barrier. Whoever is caught, has himself to blame for his death.
The same word.
The stranger the Temple would kill for stepping inside, is the one man who came back to worship.
And Jesus tells him: Arise, go thy way. Thy faith hath made thee whole.
Ten were cleansed. Only one heard those words.
